title: YOU WERE TOLD YOU ARE NO LONGER UNDER THE LAW… BUT DOES THAT MEAN YOU CAN LIVE HOWEVER YOU WANT?
paragraphs: YOU WERE TOLD YOU ARE NO LONGER UNDER THE LAW… BUT DOES THAT MEAN YOU CAN LIVE HOWEVER YOU WANT?
Jesus fulfilled the Law. Paul said we are under grace. Yet Jesus warned against setting aside God's commandments. So which commands still apply to Christians—and what happens when we get this wrong?
There is a sentence in the Bible that has set countless people free.
And that very same sentence has been used by others to justify the very sins Jesus died to save them from.
“For sin shall not have dominion over you: for ye are not under the law, but under grace.” — Romans 6:14 (KJV)
Read those words again.
Not under the Law.
Under grace.
Beautiful words. Liberating words. Words that can make a guilty soul weep with relief.
If you are no longer under the Law, does that mean God no longer cares how you live?
Can you lie because you are under grace?
Can you commit adultery because Jesus fulfilled the Law?
Can you hate your neighbor, worship money, refuse forgiveness, indulge your flesh, and dismiss conviction because salvation is not earned by obedience?
And if the answer is no, then which commandments still apply?
The Ten Commandments?
The Sabbath?
The dietary laws?
The sacrifices?
The commands about clothing, circumcision, purity, and worship?
Who decides?
Paul?
Moses?
Your pastor?
Your denomination?
Or Jesus Christ Himself?
Because somewhere between the words “Jesus paid it all” and “God expects holiness,” many sincere believers have become deeply confused.
Some are terrified that one failure will cost them their salvation.
Others have been taught that because Jesus fulfilled the Law, obedience is practically optional.
One group lives as though the cross accomplished too little.
The other risks living as though the cross demands nothing.
And both desperately need to hear what Scripture actually says.
Because the truth is more beautiful, more demanding, and more liberating than either extreme.
Jesus did not die to make sin acceptable. He died to make sinners new.
And to understand why that matters, we need to go back to a hillside in Galilee.
Imagine standing among the crowds.
The air is warm. People have traveled from surrounding villages. Some are sick. Some are exhausted. Some have spent their entire lives trying to satisfy religious expectations.
Then Jesus begins teaching.
And He says something that should settle one of the greatest misunderstandings about Christianity.
“Think not that I am come to destroy the law, or the prophets: I am not come to destroy, but to fulfil.” — Matthew 5:17 (KJV)
In the Greek text, the word translated “destroy” is καταλῦσαι (katalysai), from katalyō, meaning to tear down, dismantle, or abolish.
The word translated “fulfil” is πληρῶσαι (plērōsai), from plēroō, meaning to fulfill, complete, or bring to fullness.
Jesus was not announcing that God's previous revelation had been a mistake.
He was declaring that it was reaching its intended fulfillment in Him.
That distinction changes everything.
The Law was never a collection of random religious restrictions that God later regretted.
It revealed His holiness.
It exposed human sin.
It governed Israel's covenant life.
It established patterns of worship, sacrifice, justice, purity, and community.
And throughout its ceremonies, promises, and prophetic expectations, it pointed forward to something greater.
Someone greater.
Jesus Christ.
The Hebrew word commonly translated “law” is תּוֹרָה (torah), meaning instruction, teaching, or law.
It was God's covenant instruction to Israel, not merely a list of penalties.
But even that understanding is incomplete without recognizing where the story was heading.
Because the Law could identify sin.
It could command righteousness.
It could prescribe sacrifices.
But it could not, through human obedience, transform guilty sinners into righteous people.
And that is where the scandal begins.
The God who gave the Law entered human history in the person of His Son.
The One who never sinned stood among sinners.
The One who perfectly obeyed was condemned by lawless men.
And the One who deserved no judgment voluntarily bore the judgment our sins deserved.
At Calvary, grace did not declare sin harmless.
Grace revealed just how serious sin was—and how far God's love would go to redeem us.
But wait.
If Jesus fulfilled the Law, why did He continue by saying:
“Whosoever therefore shall break one of these least commandments, and shall teach men so, he shall be called the least in the kingdom of heaven.” — Matthew 5:19 (KJV)
That sounds very different from saying commandments no longer matter.
And it is.
Jesus was warning His listeners not to treat God's revelation as disposable.
Matthew 5:18–20 makes clear that He regarded the Law and the Prophets as enduringly significant in God's redemptive purpose.
But the rest of the New Testament also teaches that Christ's fulfillment changes how believers relate to the Mosaic covenant.
That is not a contradiction.
It is the difference between abolishing God's revelation and fulfilling the covenant to which that revelation belonged.
Consider what happened when Jesus continued His sermon.
He did not say, “You have heard that murder is wrong, but now murder is acceptable.”
Instead, He confronted the anger and contempt that grow inside the human heart.
He did not say, “Adultery no longer matters.”
He exposed the lust that can corrupt a person long before an outward act occurs.
He did not lower the moral seriousness of God's commands.
He carried their implications deeper.
Beyond appearances.
Beyond public reputation.
Beyond the carefully managed religious image.
Straight into the places we hide from everyone else.
And suddenly, the question is no longer merely whether you have broken a visible commandment.
It becomes whether your heart truly loves what God loves.
That is uncomfortable.
Because you can avoid murder while quietly nurturing hatred.
You can avoid physical adultery while feeding lust in secret.
You can appear generous while being ruled by greed.
You can attend church every Sunday while refusing to forgive someone you claim to love.
You can quote Scripture publicly while manipulating people privately.
And you can defend biblical morality while remaining completely indifferent to the suffering of your neighbor.
Jesus exposes all of it.
Not because He enjoys humiliating sinners.
But because superficial religion cannot heal what we refuse to acknowledge.
The Law can expose the wound. Only Christ can save and transform the wounded sinner.
Now return to Paul's words.
“For ye are not under the law, but under grace.”
The Greek expression in Romans 6:14 is:
οὐ γάρ ἐστε ὑπὸ νόμον ἀλλὰ ὑπὸ χάριν
ou gar este hypo nomon alla hypo charin
A close translation is:
“For you are not under law, but under grace.”
The word νόμον (nomon) means law.
The word χάριν (charin) comes from charis, meaning grace or favor.
Paul is describing a decisive change in the believer's relationship to sin, the Law, and God's saving grace.
But what does he mean?
Thankfully, Paul answers the question himself.
In the very next verse.
“What then? shall we sin, because we are not under the law, but under grace? God forbid.” — Romans 6:15 (KJV)
There it is.
The question people are still asking two thousand years later.
And Paul's answer could hardly be stronger.
The Greek expression is μὴ γένοιτο (mē genoito).
An emphatic rejection.
“Absolutely not!”
“May it never be!”
Paul anticipated the possibility that someone would turn grace into permission for sin.
And he rejected it immediately.
Why?
Because Romans 6 is not primarily about receiving permission to ignore God's will.
It is about being united with Jesus Christ in His death and resurrection.
Paul teaches that believers have died to sin's old dominion and are called to walk in newness of life.
That does not mean Christians become incapable of sinning.
It means sin no longer has the rightful claim of mastery it once exercised over them.
Grace does not simply pardon.
Grace also begins to transform.
This is where many of us need to confront an uncomfortable possibility.
We may have been asking the wrong question.
Instead of asking, “How much sin can I commit and still be saved?”
Perhaps we should ask, “If Jesus rescued me from sin, why am I trying to make peace with it?”
Because salvation is not a loophole.
It is a rescue.
Imagine a man drowning in deep water.
Someone dives in, reaches him, and carries him toward shore.
The man survives because another person saved him.
He did not earn that rescue.
He did not accomplish it through his own strength.
But imagine that after being rescued, he turns around and says:
“Since you saved me for free, I suppose I should jump back into the water and stay there.”
Something is terribly wrong with that understanding of rescue.
The rescuer did not save him because drowning was harmless.
He saved him because drowning was destroying him.
And Jesus did not come to make us comfortable in the very bondage from which He came to deliver us.
Grace is not God's permission to remain enslaved. It is God's power at work in those He has redeemed.
But this raises another difficult question.
If Christians must obey God, are we still required to keep every commandment in the Old Testament?
Here is where careful biblical interpretation matters.
And where simplistic answers can cause real spiritual damage.
The Mosaic Law was given to Israel as part of God's covenant with that nation.
It included commands concerning worship, sacrifices, priesthood, food, purity, civil justice, festivals, moral conduct, and community life.
Christians often speak of moral, ceremonial, and civil laws.
Those categories can be useful for explaining different functions of the Mosaic commandments.
But we should be careful.
The Bible does not present them as three formally separated legal codes with those exact labels.
They are theological distinctions used to help readers understand the Law's varied purposes.
And sincere Christians have differed about precisely how those distinctions should be applied.
What the New Testament clearly teaches is that Jesus Christ fulfilled the sacrificial system and inaugurated the new covenant.
Hebrews 10:1 describes the Law as having a shadow of the good things to come.
Hebrews 10:10–14 teaches that Christ's once-for-all offering accomplishes what repeated animal sacrifices could not.
Think about what that means.
You do not need to bring a lamb to an altar to obtain forgiveness.
Not because sin has become less serious.
But because the Lamb of God has come.
You do not need a succession of Levitical priests to offer sacrifices for your sins.
Not because mediation no longer matters.
But because Jesus is our great High Priest.
You do not need to repeat the old sacrificial system.
Because the sacrifice to which it pointed has been offered.
The shadow was never meant to replace the Savior.
Hebrews 8:6–13 presents Jesus as the mediator of a better covenant and describes the former covenant as becoming obsolete.
That is why Christians are not required to reconstruct ancient Israel's sacrificial and priestly system.
The new covenant is not merely the old covenant with a different name.
Something decisive has happened in Christ.
And the apostles had to confront the practical consequences.
In Acts 15, the early church faced a serious controversy.
Did Gentile believers need to be circumcised and required to keep the Law of Moses in order to belong to God's people?
The apostles and elders gathered in Jerusalem.
The question was not theoretical.
It concerned the very identity of the Gospel.
Would Gentiles be accepted through the grace of Jesus Christ?
Or would they first have to enter the Mosaic covenant through circumcision and its obligations?
Peter declared:
“But we believe that through the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ we shall be saved, even as they.” — Acts 15:11 (KJV)
The council did not require Gentile Christians to be circumcised and keep the Mosaic Law as a condition of salvation.
Instead, it gave specific instructions concerning idolatry, sexual immorality, blood, and things strangled (Acts 15:19–29).
Those instructions arose in the setting of Gentile conversion, holiness, and fellowship between Jewish and Gentile believers.
Christians have debated aspects of their continuing application, particularly the food-related restrictions.
But the council's central conclusion is unmistakable.
Gentiles do not become God's people by first becoming Jews under the Mosaic covenant. They are received through the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ.
That same truth appears in Paul's letter to the Galatians.
He strongly opposed requiring circumcision as a condition of justification.
He warned that seeking to be justified by the Law abandons reliance upon Christ's grace (Galatians 5:2–4).
But notice what he said only a few verses later.
“For, brethren, ye have been called unto liberty; only use not liberty for an occasion to the flesh, but by love serve one another.” — Galatians 5:13 (KJV)
And then:
“For all the law is fulfilled in one word, even in this; Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself.” — Galatians 5:14 (KJV)
This is extraordinary.
Paul defends freedom from the Mosaic Law as a covenantal system.
Then he immediately insists that Christian freedom must express itself through love.
Not selfishness.
Not exploitation.
Not indulgence.
Love.
The Greek word translated “serve” in Galatians 5:13 is δουλεύετε (douleuete), from douleuō, meaning to serve as a slave or be in service.
Do you see the beautiful reversal?
We are freed from sin's slavery and from the Law as the means of obtaining righteousness.
Yet we willingly serve one another in love.
Freedom in Christ is not the absence of responsibility.
It is the liberation of the heart to love God and others rightly.
And that brings us to the question many Christians have been waiting for.
So which commandments still apply?
The New Testament does not hand Christians a single replacement list that simply labels every Mosaic command “active” or “canceled.”
Instead, it teaches us to understand God's commands through Jesus Christ, His completed work, His apostles' teaching, and the new covenant.
Commands against murder, adultery, theft, lying, idolatry, and covetousness are reaffirmed as part of Christian moral life.
Jesus condemns murder, adultery, and falsehood.
Paul condemns sexual immorality, greed, idolatry, and dishonesty.
Romans 13:8–10 explicitly recalls commandments against adultery, murder, stealing, and coveting, and shows how love fulfills their righteous intent.
Ephesians 4–5 calls believers to truthfulness, forgiveness, sexual purity, kindness, and holiness.
Galatians 5:19–23 contrasts the works of the flesh with the fruit of the Spirit.
These are not optional religious preferences.
They are expressions of the life to which Christ calls His people.
But there is a crucial distinction.
Christians do not obey these commands to purchase salvation. They obey because they belong to the Savior.
Ephesians 2:8–9 declares that salvation is by grace through faith, not by works.
And the very next verse says that believers are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Do not separate what Scripture holds together.
Good works are not the price of redemption.
They are part of the purpose for which the redeemed have been made new.
The same grace that saves us also teaches us to renounce ungodliness (Titus 2:11–14).
This is why a Christian cannot reasonably say, “Since I am under grace, I have no obligation to love my neighbor.”
Love is not a minor addition to Christianity.
It is central to the life of Christ's disciples.
Jesus said:
“If ye love me, keep my commandments.” — John 14:15 (KJV)
He also commanded His disciples to love one another as He had loved them (John 13:34–35).
And after His resurrection, He commissioned them to make disciples, teaching them to observe all that He had commanded (Matthew 28:18–20).
Grace does not erase discipleship.
Grace makes genuine discipleship possible.
Now, what about the Sabbath?
This is one of the places where Christians should be especially careful not to claim more certainty than the biblical discussion permits.
The Sabbath command appears in the Ten Commandments (Exodus 20:8–11), and it was also a distinctive covenant sign between God and Israel (Exodus 31:13–17).
Jesus affirmed His authority as Lord of the Sabbath and challenged interpretations that turned it into a burden rather than a gift (Mark 2:27–28).
Yet the New Testament also records differences over the observance of particular days.
Romans 14:5–6 speaks of believers esteeming days differently while seeking to honor the Lord.
Colossians 2:16–17 warns against allowing others to judge believers concerning food, festivals, new moons, or sabbaths, describing these as shadows whose substance belongs to Christ.
Christian traditions understand the continuing Sabbath obligation differently.
Some hold that the fourth commandment remains binding as a weekly day of rest and worship, often observed on Sunday.
Others maintain that the seventh-day Sabbath remains the proper observance.
Still others understand Sabbath observance as fulfilled in Christ and do not regard a particular day as universally binding under the new covenant.
These differences deserve serious biblical study, not careless accusations against fellow believers.
What Christians should not do is use their convictions about days as an excuse to neglect worship, despise other believers, or ignore the rest and devotion that honor God.
And what about food?
Jesus' teaching in Mark 7:14–23 places profound emphasis on the uncleanness that proceeds from the human heart.
Mark 7:19 is commonly understood, particularly in many modern translations, as indicating that Jesus declared all foods clean, although the passage's wording and interpretation have been discussed.

Acts 10 uses Peter's vision involving clean and unclean animals to confront the exclusion of Gentiles, with Peter himself emphasizing that God had taught him not to call any person common or unclean (Acts 10:28).
Romans 14 addresses differences over food and urges believers not to destroy one another over disputed matters.
Colossians 2:16 likewise warns against judgment concerning food and drink.
For these reasons, most Christian traditions do not regard Israel's dietary regulations as binding covenant requirements for Christians.
But this freedom must never become an excuse for gluttony, disregard for health, or contempt toward someone whose conscience leads them to abstain.
Paul's concern is not merely what a Christian has the right to do.
It is whether that freedom is exercised in love.
And what about circumcision?
Galatians 5:6 gives a remarkably clear answer concerning its spiritual status in Christ:
“For in Jesus Christ neither circumcision availeth any thing, nor uncircumcision; but faith which worketh by love.” — Galatians 5:6 (KJV)
Circumcision is not required for justification or membership in Christ's people.
The decisive issue is not an external covenant marker.
It is faith in Jesus Christ expressing itself through love.
And what about the laws governing ancient Israel's civil penalties, land arrangements, and national institutions?
Those belonged to Israel's historical covenant administration.
Christians can still learn enduring truths about God's justice, concern for the vulnerable, honesty, fairness, and the seriousness of evil from those laws.
But the New Testament does not command the church to establish itself as a replacement nation-state and enforce the entire Mosaic civil code.
The church is called to bear witness to Christ among the nations.
To proclaim the Gospel.
To practice holiness.
To love its neighbors.
To seek justice and mercy.
To make disciples.
Not to confuse the mission of the church with the political institutions of ancient Israel.
And what about the Ten Commandments as a whole?
Christians broadly affirm their profound importance as a revelation of God's moral character and covenant instruction.
Yet traditions differ over how the Decalogue functions within the new covenant, particularly regarding the Sabbath.

It is therefore more accurate to say that Christian obedience is governed by God's will as revealed and fulfilled in Jesus Christ and taught by His apostles than to pretend that every Christian tradition agrees on one simple classification of every Old Testament command.
But do not mistake that nuance for uncertainty about the heart of Christian living.
Jesus was asked which commandment was greatest.
He answered:
“Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind.” — Matthew 22:37 (KJV)
And then:
“Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself.” — Matthew 22:39 (KJV)
He declared that all the Law and the Prophets hang upon these two commandments.
This is not permission to redefine love according to our feelings.
Biblical love is shaped by God's truth.
Love refuses to exploit.
Love refuses to betray.
Love refuses to celebrate evil.
Love seeks the good of another person.
Love speaks truth without cruelty.
Love practices mercy without pretending sin is harmless.
And love begins with wholehearted devotion to God.
The apostle Paul wrote:
“Bear ye one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ.” — Galatians 6:2 (KJV)
There is the phrase worth remembering.
The law of Christ.
Christians are not lawless.
They belong to Jesus.
They live under His lordship.
They follow His teaching.
They are led by His Spirit.
They are called to love as He loved.
And that kind of love is far more demanding than merely checking off religious requirements.
Because a checklist can sometimes be completed without compassion.
But Christlike love asks what happens when nobody is watching.
It asks how you treat the person who cannot repay you.
It asks whether you tell the truth when lying would protect your reputation.
It asks whether you forgive when resentment feels justified.
It asks whether you repent when the Holy Spirit exposes your pride.
It asks whether the Jesus you praise on Sunday is the same Jesus you obey on Monday.
And now the conversation becomes painfully personal.
Because perhaps you have spent years trying to be good enough for God.
You pray.
You attend church.
You give.
You serve.
You avoid certain sins.
But deep inside, you are exhausted.
Every mistake feels like proof that God must be disappointed in you.
Every spiritual failure sends you back into fear.
You read Romans 6:14 and desperately want to believe that grace is real.
But part of you still thinks God's love rises and falls with your performance.
If that is you, listen carefully.
Your obedience did not put Jesus on the cross, and your obedience cannot replace what He accomplished there.
You cannot earn what Christ purchased by His blood.
Romans 8:1 declares:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.” — Romans 8:1 (KJV)
That promise belongs to those who are in Christ.
Not to those who have achieved sinless perfection.
Not to those who have never struggled.
Not to those who have never needed to repent.
To those who belong to Him.
But perhaps your struggle is different.
Perhaps you have been using grace to silence conviction.
You know the relationship is sinful.
You know the habit is destroying you.
You know the dishonesty needs to stop.
You know you have been mistreating someone.
You know you have been neglecting prayer, feeding resentment, or hiding behind a public Christian identity while privately surrendering to something you refuse to confront.
And whenever conviction rises, you tell yourself:
“I'm not under the Law. I'm under grace.”
Friend, do not turn the kindness of God into an argument against the holiness of God.
Romans 2:4 teaches that God's kindness is meant to lead us to repentance.
First John 1:9 assures believers that when we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse us.
And 1 John 2:1 reminds us that if anyone sins, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous.
The Gospel gives no encouragement to despair.
But neither does it encourage us to defend the sins for which Christ died.
There is forgiveness.
There is cleansing.
There is restoration.
There is power to begin walking differently.
Not because you are strong enough to save yourself.
But because Jesus Christ is a mighty Savior.
Maybe you are reading this after failing again.
The same temptation.
The same secret compromise.
The same promise you made to God last week.
And now you feel ashamed even to pray.
You wonder whether you have exhausted His patience.
You wonder whether someone like you can still be changed.
Look at Peter.
He boldly promised loyalty.
Then denied Jesus three times.
Imagine the weight of that failure.
The sound of his own voice.
The memory of his denial.
The knowledge that he had abandoned the Lord he claimed to love.
But Peter's failure was not the end of his story.
In John 21, the risen Jesus met him again.
And three times Jesus asked Peter about his love.
The encounter was painful.
But it was restorative.
Jesus did not pretend Peter had never failed.
Nor did He declare Peter beyond redemption.
He recommissioned him.
“Feed my sheep.”
What a Savior.
The One Peter denied became the One who restored him.
And that is why the Gospel is so much more than a system of rules.
It is the announcement that the crucified and risen Jesus Christ receives repentant sinners and makes them His own.
Not because scandal is insignificant.
Not because repentance is unnecessary.
Not because obedience has been abolished.
But because Jesus rewrites what sin and shame seemed determined to make final.

The woman caught in adultery in John 8 provides another powerful picture, though the passage's manuscript history deserves an important note: John 7:53–8:11 is absent from some of the earliest surviving Greek manuscripts and is marked or discussed in many modern Bibles.
In the traditional account, Jesus refuses to join the woman's accusers in condemning her.
But He does not tell her that adultery is acceptable.
He says:
“Go, and sin no more.” — John 8:11 (KJV)
Mercy and holiness stand together.
Forgiveness and transformation belong together.
The Gospel does not say, “Your sin does not matter.”
It says, “Your sin is serious, but Christ's mercy is greater than your guilt, and His grace calls you into a new life.”
This is what happens when we stop treating Law and grace as though they are competing gods.
God is not divided against Himself.
The God who revealed His holiness through the Law is the God who revealed His saving mercy through Jesus Christ.
His moral character has not changed.
His redemptive plan has reached its fulfillment in His Son.
And the new covenant promises something astonishing.
Jeremiah 31:33 says:
“I will put my law in their inward parts, and write it in their hearts.” — Jeremiah 31:33 (KJV)
In the Hebrew text, the phrase is:
נָתַתִּי אֶת־תּוֹרָתִי בְּקִרְבָּם
natatti et-torati beqirbam
“I will put my law within them.”
And:
וְעַל־לִבָּם אֶכְתֲּבֶנָּה
ve'al-libbam ekhtavennah
“And on their heart I will write it.”
The promise is not simply that God would issue another external list.
It is that His covenant people would know Him through a transformed relationship.
Ezekiel 36:26–27 develops the same hope through the promise of a new heart and God's Spirit, who moves His people to walk in His ways.
Hebrews 8:8–12 applies Jeremiah's new-covenant promise to the work of Christ.
Do you see the wonder?
The goal of redemption is not merely to change your religious status while leaving your heart untouched.
God intends to make a people who know Him, love Him, and walk in His ways.
That transformation is not completed by human willpower.
It is the work of divine grace.
And it continues as believers repent, trust, obey, struggle, grow, and depend upon the Holy Spirit.
So when someone asks, “Are Christians still under the Law?” the biblical answer needs to be more careful than a simple slogan.

Christians are not under the Mosaic Law as the covenantal system by which they must obtain righteousness or establish their standing among God's people. They are saved by grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
But Christians are not free from God's moral will.
They are called to obey Christ, walk by the Spirit, love God and neighbor, and pursue the holiness that belongs to their new life.
The sacrificial and priestly system finds its fulfillment in Jesus.
Circumcision is not required for salvation.
The Mosaic food laws are not generally regarded as binding new-covenant obligations, though conscience and love remain important.
The civil institutions of ancient Israel are not simply transferred wholesale to the church.
Questions such as Sabbath observance require careful interpretation and charitable engagement across Christian traditions.
And the moral commands reaffirmed and deepened through Christ and His apostles remain essential to Christian discipleship.
Not as a ladder by which sinners climb into heaven.
But as part of the life of those whom grace has rescued.
This is the balance we must never lose.
We are not saved because we obey. But saving grace does not leave us indifferent to obedience.
And even that sentence needs one more truth.
Our obedience will never become the foundation of our confidence before God.
Jesus Christ remains that foundation.
On your strongest spiritual day, you still need His grace.
On your weakest spiritual day, His invitation to repent and trust Him still matters.
You never graduate beyond the cross.
You never outgrow your need for mercy.
And you never become so spiritually mature that you can safely ignore His commands.
The Christian life is not a choice between grace and holiness.
It is a life in which grace produces the desire and strength to pursue holiness.
And perhaps this is where the real question finally emerges.
Not, “Which commands can I stop obeying?”
But, “Lord Jesus, what would it look like for every part of my life to belong to You?”
My thoughts.
My marriage.
My sexuality.
My money.
My conversations.
My private habits.
My ambitions.
My bitterness.
My worship.
My relationships.
My treatment of strangers.
My response when I am wrong.
My willingness to forgive.
My willingness to tell the truth.
My willingness to surrender what I have been defending.
Because Christianity is not simply agreeing with a doctrine about grace.
It is trusting the Savior who gives that grace.
And when His Word confronts something in us, we do not need to run away.
We can come into the light.
We can confess.
We can repent.
We can ask for help.
We can begin again.
Not by pretending we are already perfect.
But by trusting the One who is.
If this message exposed a place where you have been confusing grace with permission, or obedience with earning God's love, do not bury that conviction.
Bring it to Jesus.
“Lord Jesus, teach me to walk in Your grace and truth.”
You do not need to share private details. Sometimes a few honest words are enough to invite another believer to stand with you in prayer.
And if you have experienced Christ's forgiveness after a season of rebellion, your testimony may encourage someone who believes restoration is no longer possible.
Tell us what Jesus has been teaching you.
Because somewhere in this community, another person may be facing the same battle you thought you were fighting alone.
If you know a believer who is exhausted from trying to earn salvation, send this article to them.
One thoughtful share may place the Gospel before someone who would never search for a sermon, open a Christian book, or enter a church building.
Return to Romans 6, Matthew 5, Galatians 5, Acts 15, and Hebrews 8–10. Read them in their full context. Test what you have read against Scripture.
Never allow even a moving Christian article to replace your own faithful study of God's Word.
Because discipleship is not meant to be a single emotional moment.
It is a lifelong journey of learning to follow Jesus.
Not because a monthly payment earns God's favor.
You glorify God through faith in Christ and a life shaped by love, truth, worship, generosity, and obedience.
Second Corinthians 9:7 teaches that giving should not be reluctant or compelled, because God loves a cheerful giver.
So please hear the invitation in that spirit.

If this ministry has helped you understand Scripture, encouraged you to repent, strengthened your faith, or pointed you back to Jesus when your heart was growing cold, consider helping us carry that message further.
Not under pressure.
Not out of guilt.
But from a willing heart.
Those resources and products can be meaningful reminders of biblical truth, but they are never the measure of someone's faith.
It is about pointing people to the One who saves.
Jesus Christ.
The Savior who fulfilled the Law.
The Redeemer who bore our sins.
The risen Lord who calls us to follow Him.
The One who does not ask us to purchase grace, but to receive it through faith.
And the One whose grace never gives us permission to abandon Him.
Before you leave, remember this.
When Jesus died on the cross, He did not cry, “You must finish paying for your salvation.”
He cried:
“It is finished.” — John 19:30 (KJV)
The Greek word is τετέλεσται (tetelestai), from teleō, meaning to finish, accomplish, or bring to completion.
In John's account, Jesus' cry declares the completion of the work He came to accomplish.
It does not mean that repentance, discipleship, and obedience no longer matter.
It means that His saving work is sufficient and cannot be improved upon by our attempts to earn redemption.
And because He rose again, those who belong to Him are called to walk in newness of life.
Not to return to bondage.
Not to live under condemnation.
Not to disguise rebellion as freedom.
But to follow Him.
So come to Christ if you have never truly trusted Him.
Return to Him if you have wandered.
Confess what you have hidden.
Receive the forgiveness He offers.
And learn to walk by His Spirit, one day at a time.
Because the final question is not whether you can find a commandment that permits you to keep your favorite sin.
The question is whether you have encountered the Savior whose grace is powerful enough to change what you once believed could never change.
The Law exposed the guilt you could not erase. Grace brought you to the Savior who could—and the hands that bore your judgment are the same hands inviting you into a new life.
